extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, critics, and students of dramatic poetry/theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating classical tragic poetry/plays, focusing on plot structure (plot vs. unravelling), episodes, chorus, and types of tragedy. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics with examples and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: general and universal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fable is general and universal; there is neither Name, Country, or Person, and the poet may give what he pleases to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject (fable) should state a general action rather than rely on particular names/places. Keep the action universal so it can represent types and be adaptable; avoid making the fable dependent on specific proper nouns or narrowly local detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be parts of the action (integrated episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Episodes are not added to the principal Action, but only dilate and increase that principal Action; each part of the fable, told singly, is matter for an episode but must be related with all circumstanes so as to be thereby rendered proper and necessary to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make episodes subordinate and contributory to the main action rather than extraneous set-pieces. Example of good practice: Homer made adventures (Polyphemus, Circe, Sirens, etc.) into necessary parts of the Odyssey's action. Anti-pattern: inserting episodes that do not advance or enlarge the principal action, or which feel grafted-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy composed of Plot and Unravelling (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole Tragedy is composed of a Plot and the Unravelling of it: the Plot is all that part from the beginning to the place where affairs change their face; the Unravelling (catastrophe) is all that is from that change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning a tragedy, explicitly separate the portion that builds suspense and obstacles (plot) from the portion that resolves them (unravelling). Use the boundary (point of change) to structure acts/scenes. Example: in Theodectes' Lynceus, the plot runs to the taking of the prince, the unravelling begins with the child's complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must contain the obstacles and hold the audience's suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot comprehends all the obstacles which traverse the designs of the principal person(s); it generally takes in the four first Acts and sometimes the greatest part of the fifth; the plot lasts so long that the spectator is in suspense concerning the issue of his hero's designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a substantial, sustained plot portion that keeps the audience in suspense. A plot that finishes too early makes the remainder dull. Example of better practice: Racine's Iphigenia and Phaedra keep the plot until late, making the resolution finer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unravelling must follow naturally and be concise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unravelling ought to be a necessary or a probable consequence of all that preceded; the shorter and quicker turn it has, the more agreeable, provided it be not precipitate and deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the catastrophe flows inevitably (or plausibly) from prior events; avoid dragging the resolution or making it abrupt/insufficient. Anti-patterns include unprepared resolutions, obscurity, excessive length, or a 'double' unravelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make a tragedy an epic complication (avoid multiplicity of fables)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Epic Complication — a complication of several fables (as if all the Iliad were put into one tragedy) — is vicious in Tragedy because tragedy's brevity does not allow every part to receive its just magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cramming many independent stories/fables into one tragedy; select a single action or a small, coherent set of incidents that can attain proper magnitude within a short dramatic span. Example/anti-pattern: attempts to put the entire destruction of Troy into one play led to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes in tragedy must be short and proportionate
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy the episodes are short; epopoeia (epic) can be extended by many episodes because of its length, but tragedy cannot afford multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep episodic material brief and tightly bound to the main action; resist transferring epic-style long episodes into drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must function as an actor and advance the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus must also take the part of an Actor, so that it makes one of the whole, and sing nothing but what is agreeable to the Subject, and which concurs with the advancement of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate the chorus into the dramatic fabric: its songs and interventions should comment on or move the action forward. Anti-pattern: choruses that sing foreign or adventitious songs unrelated to the subject (a fault attributed to Agathon and criticized in Euripides' practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action: episodes and parts must belong to the same action
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of the Fable, even foreign incidents the poet draws in, should be so appropriated to the Action that they seem proper and necessary; the unravelling, like an episode, ought always to arise naturally from the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve unity by ensuring all incidents and episodes are members of the same action. When borrowing foreign obstacles, integrate them so they serve the principal design rather than distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge sameness/difference by Plot and Unravelling, not mere Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to say a piece is the same as or different from another because the Subject is the same or different; it is more reasonable to compare the Plot and the Unravelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing works or assessing originality, focus on the arrangement of events (plot/unravelling) rather than shared subjects or myths. Examples: Sophocles and Corneille both wrote on Oedipus but produced very different plays because their plots/unravellings differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to master several tragic 'sorts' (or at least the principal ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four sorts of Tragedy (implex, simple, pathetick, moral); a poet should endeavour to succeed in all these four sorts, or at least in the greatest part of them and the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate versatility across tragic forms: empl ex (with peripety & remembrance), simple, pathetick (with deaths/wounds/passion), and moral (moral reformation, happy catastrophe). If you cannot master all, aim for excellence in the most relevant kinds for your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of tragic sorts: implex vs simple; pathetick vs moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Implex Tragedy consists in peripetie and remembrance; Simple has neither and exposes the subject as it goes on. Pathetick are those with passions (deaths, wounds, torments); Moral are those aimed to reform manners and often end happily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the sort according to subject-matter and intended effect. Examples: Sophocles' Ajax is simple and pathetick; Oedipus is implex and pathetick; Prometheus is simple and pathetick; some pieces (Euripides) lean moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last (unravelling) act requires the greatest care
rubrics_metrics.description: Most poets, after they have laid the Plot well, unravel it very ill; the Poet ought to employ all his ingenuity in the Unravelling of the Plot, for that is the part of the fable which requires the greatest care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devote exceptional craft to the resolution — it determines audience judgement. Anti-pattern: a strong early plot undone by a weak, dull, or poorly prepared catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign/forreign obstacles can be used but must be appropriated
rubrics_metrics.description: The incidents which happen without (foreign) and very often part of those which the poet draws from the subject make the Plot; although foreign, the poet so appropriates them to the Action that they seem to be proper and necessary parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may introduce external incidents, but adapt them so they naturally serve the principal action. Example: some Iliad/Odyssey incidents are foreign yet in Homer they are made necessary to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid servile imitation; do not follow an author word-for-word
rubrics_metrics.description: A public Theme will then your own become, if you follow your author not too closely; not bound him word by word, nicely to trace — else your imitation will lose beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or imitating models, keep enough freedom to add grace and make the piece your own. Horace's aphorism is cited: imitation should not be literal slavish copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and choose stylistic character (rude, florid, mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three differences distinguishing writers: the rude/neglected (passions better noted), the smooth/florid (art hides nature), and the mean (a middle, composed of the best of both). The mean is most estimable and fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an authorial character suited to your aims; the balanced 'mean' style (mixing natural passion and artful diction) is often most productive. Examples: Aeschylus = rude, Euripides = smooth/florid, Sophocles = mean/mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common parts of tragedy: Subject, Sentiments, and Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the seven parts Aristotle names, only three are common to all tragedies in general: the Subject, the Sentiments, and the Diction (excluding decoration and music).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the central concerns of any tragedy are a strong subject, suitable emotional content (sentiments), and appropriate diction/style. Other elements (peripety, recognition, passion, manners) vary with the sort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vices of unravelling to avoid: ill-prepared, too long, obscure, double
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unravelling is often vicious because it is not well prepared and does not proceed from the bottom of the fable; or because it's too long and embarrassed; or because it is obscure; or because it is double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose and remove these vices: prepare causal ground for the resolution, cut superfluous length, clarify revelations, and avoid convoluted or multiple resolutions that undermine coherence.
